The United States has not had to fight any serious war since that period. So, to judge what sacrifices democratic nations may impose on themselves, we must wait until the American people is obliged to place half of its total income at the disposal of the government, as the English were, or until it sends a twentieth of its population onto the battlefield, as France did. *q
q [ [The Civil War showed that when necessity arose, the American people, in the North and in the South alike, were capable of making the most enormous sacrifices, both in money and in men.]]

In America conscription is unknown, and men are persuaded to enlist by bounties. The ideas and habits of the people of the United States are so opposed to compulsory enlistment that I do not think it can ever be sanctioned by the laws. What the French call the conscription is certainly the heaviest tax on the population of that country; yet how could a great continental war be fought without it? The Americans have not adopted the British practice of pressing seamen into service, and they have nothing like the French system of maritime conscription. The navy, like the merchant service, is staffed by volunteers. But it is hard to see how a nation could sustain a great naval war without resorting to one or the other of these two systems. Indeed, the Union, which has fought with some distinction at sea, has never had a very large fleet, and equipping the small number of American ships has always been extremely expensive.

I have heard American statesmen admit that the Union will have great difficulty keeping its rank at sea unless it adopts impressment or maritime conscription. But the difficulty is to get the people, who hold the supreme authority, to submit to impressment or to any compulsory system.

It is beyond dispute that in times of danger a free people shows far more energy than one that is not free. But I am inclined to think that this is especially true of those free nations in which the democratic element predominates. Democracy seems to me much better suited to the peaceful running of society, or to an occasional effort of remarkable vigor, than to the hardy and prolonged endurance of the storms that beset the political existence of nations. The reason is plain. Enthusiasm prompts men to expose themselves to dangers and privations, but they will not bear these for long without reflection. There is more calculation, even in the impulses of courage, than people generally suppose. The first efforts are inspired by passion, but perseverance is kept up by a clear view of the goal. We risk a part of what we value in order to save the rest.

But it is just this clear perception of the future, founded on sound judgment and informed experience, that democracies most often lack. The populace is more inclined to feel than to reason, and if its present sufferings are great, it is to be feared that the still greater sufferings that come with defeat will be forgotten.

Another cause tends to make the efforts of a democratic government less persevering than those of an aristocracy. The lower classes are not only less alert than the higher orders to the good or bad chances of the future, but they also suffer far more keenly from present privations. The nobleman does risk his life, but the chance of glory is as great as the chance of harm. If he gives up a large part of his income to the State, he deprives himself for a time of the pleasures of wealth. But for the poor man, death is adorned with no pomp or renown, and the taxes that are irksome to the rich are fatal to him.

This relative weakness of democratic republics is perhaps the greatest obstacle to founding a republic of this kind in Europe. For such a State to survive in one country of the Old World, similar institutions would have to be introduced into all the other nations.

I believe that a democratic government tends in the end to increase the real strength of society. But it can never gather as much power at a single point and at a given moment as an aristocracy or a monarchy can. If a democratic country lived under a republican government for a whole century, it would probably be more populous and more prosperous at the end of that time than the neighboring despotic States. But it would have run the risk of being conquered much more often than they would in that span of years.
Self-Control of the American Democracy
The American people accepts slowly, or often does not accept, what is good for its own interests — The faults of the American democracy are for the most part reparable.

A democracy has difficulty mastering its passions and setting aside the demands of the moment for the sake of the future, and this shows even in the most trivial events in the United States. The people, surrounded by flatterers, finds it very hard to overcome its inclinations. Whenever it is asked to accept a privation or any kind of inconvenience, even to reach a goal that its own reason approves, it almost always refuses at first. The Americans’ deference to the laws has been justly praised. But it must be added that in America legislation is made by the people and for the people. As a result, in the United States the law favors the very classes that elsewhere have the greatest interest in evading it. It may therefore be supposed that an onerous law, one not recognized as being of immediate usefulness, would either not be passed or not be obeyed.

In America there is no law against fraudulent bankruptcies. This is not because they are few, but because bankruptcies are so numerous. The fear of being prosecuted as a bankrupt weighs more heavily on the minds of most people than the fear of being dragged into losses or ruin by other people’s failures. And the public conscience extends a kind of guilty tolerance to an offense that everyone condemns as an individual. In the new States of the Southwest, the citizens generally take justice into their own hands, and murders are very frequent. This comes from the rough customs and the ignorance of the inhabitants of those wilderness regions, who do not see the use of giving the law adequate force and who prefer duels to prosecutions.

Someone remarked to me one day in Philadelphia that almost all crimes in America are caused by the abuse of strong liquor, which the lower classes can get in great abundance because it is so extremely cheap. “How is it,” I said, “that you do not put a duty on brandy?” “Our legislators,” my informant replied, “have often thought of this remedy. But putting it into effect is difficult. A revolt might be feared, and the members who voted for such a law would be sure to lose their seats.” “From which I am to infer,” I answered, “that the drinking population is the majority in your country, and that temperance is somewhat unpopular.”

When these things are pointed out to American statesmen, they simply assure you that time will bring about the necessary change and that the experience of evil will teach the people where its true interests lie. This is often true. A democracy is more liable to error than a monarch or a body of nobles, but its chances of regaining the right path once it has recognized its mistake are also greater. For it is rarely hampered by internal interests that conflict with those of the majority and resist the authority of reason. But a democracy can arrive at the truth only through experience, and many nations may lose their existence while they wait for the consequences of their errors.

The great privilege of the Americans lies not simply in being better educated than other nations, but in being able to repair the faults they may commit. It must be added that a democracy cannot gain real benefit from past experience unless it has reached a certain level of knowledge and civilization. There are tribes and peoples whose education has been so bad, and whose character is such a strange mixture of passion, ignorance, and mistaken ideas on every subject, that they cannot see the causes of their own misery, and they fall victim to ills they do not understand.

I have crossed vast tracts of country that were once inhabited by powerful Native American nations which are now extinct. I have myself spent some time among the shattered tribes that witness the daily decline of their numbers and of the glory of their independence, and I have heard these Native Americans themselves foresee the doom that hangs over their race. Every European can see means that would rescue these unfortunate people from certain destruction. They alone fail to see the remedy. They feel the woe that year after year heaps on their heads, but they will perish to the last man without accepting the cure. It would be necessary to use force to make them submit to the protection and the constraint of civilization.

The endless revolutions that have convulsed the South American provinces for the last quarter of a century have often been mentioned with astonishment, and people have expected those nations soon to return to their natural state. But can it be said that the turmoil of revolution is not in fact the most natural state of the South American Spaniards at present? In that country society is plunged into difficulties from which all its efforts are powerless to rescue it. The inhabitants of that fair portion of the Western Hemisphere seem obstinately bent on pursuing the work of internal destruction. If exhaustion brings them a moment of rest, that rest only prepares them for a fresh frenzy. When I consider their condition, which alternates between misery and crime, I would be inclined to believe that despotism itself would be a benefit to them, if the words despotism and benefit could ever be joined in my mind.
Conduct of Foreign Affairs by the American Democracy

Direction given to the foreign policy of the United States by Washington and Jefferson — Almost all the defects inherent in democratic institutions come to light in the conduct of foreign affairs — Their advantages are less noticeable.

We have seen that the Federal Constitution entrusts the lasting direction of the nation’s external interests to the President and the Senate, *r which to some extent removes the Union’s general foreign policy from the people’s control. It cannot therefore be said with truth that the State’s external affairs are conducted by the democracy.

r [ “The President,” says the Constitution, Art. II, sect. 2, Section 2, “shall have power, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate, to make treaties, provided two-thirds of the senators present concur.” The reader is reminded that the senators are elected for a term of six years and that they are chosen by the legislature of each State.]

The policy of America owes its origin to Washington, and after him to Jefferson, who established the principles that it follows today. Washington said, in the admirable letter he addressed to his fellow citizens, which may be regarded as his political legacy to the country: “The great rule of conduct for us in regard to foreign nations is, in extending our commercial relations, to have with them as little political connection as possible. So far as we have already formed engagements, let them be fulfilled with perfect good faith. Here let us stop. Europe has a set of primary interests which to us have none, or a very remote relation. Hence, she must be engaged in frequent controversies, the causes of which are essentially foreign to our concerns. Hence, therefore, it must be unwise in us to implicate ourselves, by artificial ties, in the ordinary vicissitudes of her politics, or the ordinary combinations and collisions of her friendships or enmities. Our detached and distant situation invites and enables us to pursue a different course. If we remain one people, under an efficient government, the period is not far off when we may defy material injury from external annoyance; when we may take such an attitude as will cause the neutrality we may at any time resolve upon to be scrupulously respected; when belligerent nations, under the impossibility of making acquisitions upon us, will not lightly hazard the giving us provocation; when we may choose peace or war, as our interest, guided by justice, shall counsel. Why forego the advantages of so peculiar a situation? Why quit our own to stand upon foreign ground? Why, by interweaving our destiny with that of any part of Europe, entangle our peace and prosperity in the toils of European ambition, rivalship, interest, humor, or caprice? It is our true policy to steer clear of permanent alliances with any portion of the foreign world; so far, I mean, as we are now at liberty to do it; for let me not be understood as capable of patronizing infidelity to existing engagements. I hold the maxim no less applicable to public than to private affairs, that honesty is always the best policy. I repeat it; therefore, let those engagements be observed in their genuine sense; but in my opinion it is unnecessary, and would be unwise, to extend them. Taking care always to keep ourselves, by suitable establishments, in a respectable defensive posture, we may safely trust to temporary alliances for extraordinary emergencies.” Earlier in the same letter, Washington makes this admirable and just remark: “The nation which indulges toward another an habitual hatred or an habitual fondness is in some degree a slave. It is a slave to its animosity or to its affection, either of which is sufficient to lead it astray from its duty and its interest.”

Washington’s political conduct was always guided by these maxims. He succeeded in keeping his country at peace while all the other nations of the globe were at war, and he laid it down as a fundamental doctrine that the true interest of the Americans lay in perfect neutrality toward the internal quarrels of the European powers.

Jefferson went further still, and introduced into the policy of the Union a maxim which holds that “the Americans ought never to solicit any privileges from foreign nations, in order not to be obliged to grant similar privileges themselves.”

These two principles were so plain and so sound that even the populace could grasp them, and they have greatly simplified the foreign policy of the United States. Since the Union takes no part in the affairs of Europe, it has, properly speaking, no foreign interests to deal with, for it has at present no powerful neighbors on the American continent. The country is as far removed from the passions of the Old World by its position as by the policy it has chosen. It is not called upon either to reject or to embrace the conflicting interests of Europe, while the quarrels of the New World still lie hidden in the future.

The Union is free of all earlier obligations, and so it can profit from the experience of the old nations of Europe. It does not have to make the best of the past and adapt it to present circumstances, as they do, or to accept the immense inheritance they receive from their forefathers, an inheritance of glory mixed with calamities and of alliances at odds with national antipathies. By its very nature, the foreign policy of the United States is reduced to waiting for the chances of the nation’s future history, and for the present it consists more in refraining from interference than in taking action.

It is therefore very hard to say, at present, how much sagacity the American democracy will show in conducting the country’s foreign policy. On this point both its adversaries and its advocates must suspend judgment. As for myself, I do not hesitate to state my conviction that it is above all in the conduct of foreign relations that democratic governments seem to me decidedly inferior to governments run on different principles. Experience, instruction, and habit can almost always succeed in giving democracies a kind of practical discretion, and that knowledge of the daily events of life which is called good sense. Good sense may be enough to direct the ordinary course of society, and among a people whose education has been provided for, the advantages of democratic liberty in the country’s internal affairs may more than make up for the evils inherent in a democratic government. But this is not always so in the relations between foreign nations.

Foreign policy demands almost none of the qualities that a democracy possesses, and it requires, on the contrary, the full use of almost all the faculties in which a democracy is deficient. Democracy favors the growth of the State’s internal resources. It tends to spread a moderate independence. It promotes the growth of public spirit and strengthens respect for law in all classes of society. These are advantages that influence the relations of one people with another only indirectly. But a democracy is unable to manage the details of an important undertaking, to persevere in a design, and to carry it out in the face of serious obstacles. It cannot combine its measures with secrecy, and it will not wait patiently for their results. These are qualities that belong especially to an individual or to an aristocracy, and they are precisely the means by which a particular people attains a dominant position.

Look instead at the natural defects of aristocracy, and we find that their effect is comparatively harmless in directing a State’s external affairs. The chief fault with which aristocratic bodies can be charged is that they tend to serve their own advantage rather than that of the mass of the people. In foreign politics it is rare for the aristocracy’s interest to differ in any way from the people’s.

The tendency of democracies to obey the impulse of passion rather than the counsels of prudence, and to abandon a mature design to gratify a momentary whim, was very clearly seen in America when the French Revolution broke out. It was as obvious then as it is today, even to the simplest mind, that the interest of the Americans forbade them to take any part in the contest that was about to flood Europe with blood, but that could in no way harm the welfare of their own country. Nevertheless, the sympathies of the people declared themselves so violently on the side of France that nothing but the inflexible character of Washington and his immense popularity could have kept the Americans from declaring war on England. And even so, the efforts that the austere reason of that great man made to restrain the generous but imprudent passions of his fellow citizens very nearly cost him the one reward he had ever claimed, his country’s love. The majority then condemned the policy he adopted, which the nation has since approved unanimously. *s If the Constitution and the public’s favor had not entrusted the direction of the country’s foreign affairs to Washington, it is certain that the American nation would at that time have taken the very measures that it now condemns.

s [ See the fifth volume of Marshall’s “Life of Washington.” In a government constituted like that of the United States, he says, “it is impossible for the chief magistrate, however firm he may be, to oppose for any length of time the torrent of popular opinion; and the prevalent opinion of that day seemed to incline to war. In fact, in the session of Congress held at the time, it was frequently seen that Washington had lost the majority in the House of Representatives.” The violence of the language used against him in public was extreme, and at a political meeting they did not hesitate to compare him indirectly to the traitor Arnold. “By the opposition,” says Marshall, “the friends of the administration were declared to be an aristocratic and corrupt faction, who, from a desire to introduce monarchy, were hostile to France and under the influence of Britain; that they were a paper nobility, whose extreme sensibility at every measure which threatened the funds, induced a tame submission to injuries and insults, which the interests and honor of the nation required them to resist.”]

Almost all the nations that have ever had a powerful influence on the destinies of the world, by conceiving, pursuing, and carrying out vast designs, from the Romans to the English, have been governed by aristocratic institutions. This will not surprise us when we remember that nothing in the world holds to its purpose so firmly as an aristocracy. The mass of the people may be led astray by ignorance or passion. A king’s mind may be swayed, and his perseverance in his designs may be shaken; besides, a king is not immortal. But an aristocratic body is too numerous to be misled by the blandishments of intrigue, and yet not numerous enough to yield easily to the intoxicating influence of thoughtless passion. It has the energy of a firm and well-informed individual, added to the power it draws from perpetuity.
